generations.name: First generation (YJ)
generations.note: Square headlights, leaf springs, and a controversy that never fully died. The 4.0L straight-six from 1991 is the engine to have; the four-cylinder is the one to budget around.

generations.name: Second generation (TJ)
generations.note: Round headlights back, coil springs in, and the Rubicon trim arrived in 2003 with factory lockers and a 4:1 transfer case. The TJ is the sweet spot between trail rig and usable vehicle.

generations.name: Fourth generation (JL)
generations.note: An eight-speed automatic, available diesel and plug-in hybrid 4xe versions, and a 392 V8 model with 470 hp that exists purely because Jeep could. Still body-on-frame, still a removable roof.

models.intro: The direct descendant of the Willys MB that won a war, carried through the CJ line and renamed Wrangler in 1987. Solid axles, a folding windshield, doors that come off, the formula has survived four corporate owners because altering it would end the business.
models.name: Wrangler

generations.name: First generation (ZJ)
generations.note: Bob Lutz famously drove one up the Detroit auto show steps and through a plate-glass window in 1992. UniFrame construction, full-time 4WD options, and a 5.9 Limited in 1998 that was genuinely quick.

generations.name: Fourth generation (WK2)
generations.note: Independent suspension all round and real interior quality. The range ran from a 290 hp V6 to the 707 hp supercharged Trackhawk, the WK2 covered more ground than any SUV line before or since.

generations.name: Fifth generation (WL)
generations.note: First Grand Cherokee with a three-row version (the L), plus a 4xe plug-in hybrid. The V8 is fading out of the range, which tells you where this segment is going.

models.intro: The SUV that took Jeep upmarket. The Grand Cherokee created the premium 4x4 niche in 1993, proper off-road hardware under a vehicle you'd park at a hotel, and Range Rover has been answering it ever since.

models.collectorNote: CJ-5s and CJ-7s are the usable classics, parts are everywhere and values stay sane. Early CJ-2As in original condition are the historically significant ones. Rust in the tub decides value more than anything mechanical.

generations.name: CJ-2A
generations.note: The first civilian Jeep, sold from 1945 as a farm and work vehicle, PTO outputs, a drawbar, and the Go Devil four-cylinder carried straight over from the wartime MB.

generations.name: CJ-5
generations.note: Twenty-nine years in production with only detail changes, the longest run of any Jeep model. Rounder body over the same wartime bones, with V8 power available in the 1970s.

generations.name: CJ-7
generations.note: Ten inches longer in the wheelbase than the CJ-5, an optional automatic, and Quadratrac full-time 4WD. The last CJ, and for most buyers the best one to actually own.

models.intro: CJ stands for Civilian Jeep, the Willys MB demobbed in 1945 and sold to farmers, surveyors, and anyone who needed to get somewhere roads didn't go. The CJ-5 alone ran for 29 years, and every Wrangler since is this shape with better manners.
models.name: CJ (Civilian Jeep)

generations.name: First generation (SJ)
generations.note: Designed by Brooks Stevens, launched in 1963, and sold with detail updates until 1991. The wood-panelled Grand Wagoneer of 1984–1991 invented the luxury SUV before the term existed, it's why restored examples now clear six figures.

generations.name: Revival (WS)
generations.note: Three rows, twin-turbo straight-six power, and pricing that runs deep into six figures in Grand Wagoneer form. An electric Wagoneer S sits alongside as a separate, smaller model.

models.intro: The original luxury SUV. The SJ Wagoneer arrived in 1963, predating the Range Rover by seven years, and its wood-sided Grand Wagoneer finale became the Hamptons driveway default. Jeep revived the name in 2022 as a three-row flagship.
